technical.q: What is the difference between a list and a tuple in Python? When would you use each?
points: lists are mutable, tuples are immutable
tuples can be dictionary keys / hashed, lists cannot
lists suit data that changes; tuples suit fixed records like coordinates

followups.q: A tuple containing a list — is that tuple really immutable? What can still change?
Why exactly can a list not be used as a dictionary key, while a tuple can?

technical.q: If I write a = [1, 2], then b = a, then b.append(3) — what is a afterwards, and why?
points: b is the same object as a, not a copy
a becomes [1, 2, 3]
assignment binds a name to an object; use list(a), a[:] or copy() for a real copy

followups.q: Now the list contains a nested list and I use copy.copy(). What is still shared, and how does deepcopy differ?
How would you make b an independent copy so changing it never touches a?

technical.q: What goes wrong with def add_item(item, box=[]) — a mutable default argument — and how do you fix it?
points: the default is created once, when the function is defined
the same list is shared across calls, so items leak between calls
fix: default to None and create the list inside the function

followups.q: Why does Python evaluate defaults once at definition time instead of on every call?
Show me the standard fix — what does the signature and the first lines look like?

technical.q: What is the difference between == and is in Python? When must you use is?
points: == compares values, is compares identity (same object)
interning makes small ints and short strings sometimes identical — an implementation detail, not a guarantee
use is for None and singletons; == for value comparison

followups.q: Why might x = 1000; y = 1000 give x is y as False while 10 is 10 gives True?
In plain words: what does each operator actually compare?

technical.q: What is the difference between d[key] and d.get(key) for a dictionary? When do you prefer get?
points: d[key] raises KeyError when the key is missing
get returns None or a supplied default instead of raising
get suits optional keys and counting patterns like counts.get(k, 0)

followups.q: What does setdefault do that get does not, and when is that the better tool?
What exactly does get return when the key is absent and no default is given?

technical.q: What is a generator in Python, and what problem does it solve compared with building a list?
points: generators produce values lazily, one at a time, using yield
memory stays roughly constant instead of holding the whole sequence
a generator is a one-pass iterator — it is exhausted after one full pass

followups.q: When would a generator actually be the wrong choice — what operations does it not support?
What does the yield keyword do to a function's execution when it is reached?

technical.q: Which values are falsy in Python, and what does short-circuit evaluation mean for and / or?
points: falsy: False, None, 0, empty string, empty list/dict/set
and / or return one of their operands, not always True or False
evaluation stops as soon as the result is decided — the right side may never run

followups.q: What does the expression x or 'default' actually return when x is an empty string, and why is that useful?
Give me an example where short-circuiting prevents an error.

technical.q: Explain *args and **kwargs. What types do they collect into, and what ordering rules apply in a call?
points: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple
**kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict
order in a definition: positional, *args, keyword-only, **kwargs; unpacking with * and ** also works in calls

followups.q: How do you force an argument to be keyword-only, and why would an API designer do that?
If a caller passes name='x', age=3 — where do those land, and in what data structure?

technical.q: What is the difference between a class attribute and an instance attribute in Python?
points: class attributes are shared by all instances and live on the class
instance attributes belong to one object and shadow the class attribute of the same name
mutating a mutable class attribute through an instance changes it for everyone

followups.q: When is a shared class attribute actually the right design, rather than a bug waiting to happen?
If I read obj.x and the instance has no x, where does Python look next?

technical.q: Explain inheritance in Python. What does super() do, and when would you choose composition instead?
points: a subclass reuses and extends a parent class (is-a relationship)
super() calls the parent implementation, e.g. parent __init__ or an overridden method
composition (has-a) is looser and avoids deep hierarchies when there is no true is-a relationship

followups.q: What can go wrong with a deep inheritance hierarchy as a codebase grows?
Inside a child's __init__, what exactly does super().__init__() run?

technical.q: Python has no true private variables. How is encapsulation usually done, and what does @property add?
points: a single underscore is a convention: internal, touch at your own risk
double underscore triggers name mangling — it is about avoiding subclass clashes, not real privacy
@property turns attribute access into a method call, allowing validation while keeping the .attr syntax

followups.q: Why does Python prefer convention over enforced privacy — what is the philosophy behind it?
With a property setter, what can you enforce that a plain attribute cannot?

technical.q: What are dunder methods? Contrast __str__ and __repr__, and say what __eq__ changes by default.
points: dunder methods hook objects into Python's protocols (len, str, +, ==, iteration)
__str__ is the human-readable form; __repr__ is the developer/debug form and should be unambiguous
by default == is identity; defining __eq__ compares by value — and makes instances unhashable unless __hash__ is also defined

followups.q: Why does defining __eq__ set __hash__ to None, and what breaks when you then put objects in a set?
When you print a list of your objects, which of the two methods does Python actually call on each?

technical.q: What is the MRO in Python, and how does it solve the diamond problem in multiple inheritance?
points: the Method Resolution Order is the linearised order Python searches classes for a method
Python uses C3 linearisation, which keeps local precedence and monotonicity
in a diamond, each class is visited exactly once, so the shared ancestor's method runs once via cooperative super()

followups.q: What makes multiple inheritance cooperative — what must every class in the chain do with super()?
How can you inspect a class's MRO at runtime?

technical.q: Contrast instance methods, @classmethod and @staticmethod. When is each the right choice?
points: instance methods receive self and work on one object's state
classmethod receives cls — used for alternative constructors / factory methods
staticmethod receives neither — a namespaced function that logically belongs to the class

followups.q: Why does a classmethod factory behave better than a plain constructor when subclasses get involved?
Give me a concrete factory example — what would the classmethod's body look like?

technical.q: For a Python list, what is the time complexity of append, indexing lst[i], insert(0, x), and checking x in lst?
points: append is amortised O(1); indexing is O(1)
insert at the front is O(n) — every element shifts
membership test is O(n) — it scans until it finds the value

followups.q: If you need a queue with fast pops from the front, what do you use instead of a list, and why?
Why is inserting at the front expensive while appending is cheap — what physically happens in memory?

technical.q: How does a Python dictionary find a value by key so fast? What can make it slow down?
points: the key is hashed and the hash picks a bucket/slot — average lookup O(1)
collisions (different keys, same slot) must be resolved and degrade lookups
keys must be hashable/immutable; worst case degrades toward O(n)

followups.q: Why must dictionary keys be immutable — what breaks if a key changes after insertion?
Walk me through a lookup step by step, from d[k] to the value.

technical.q: Stack versus queue: what is the ordering difference, and what does Python offer for each?
points: stack is LIFO (last in, first out); queue is FIFO (first in, first out)
a list works as a stack with append/pop at the end
use collections.deque for a queue — popleft is O(1), while list.pop(0) is O(n)

followups.q: Name one real algorithm that needs a stack and one that needs a queue.
Why is list.pop(0) slow, exactly?

technical.q: What must be true of the data for binary search to work, and why is it O(log n)?
points: the data must be sorted (on the key being searched)
each comparison discards half the remaining range
the range halves every step, so the number of steps grows logarithmically

followups.q: Your array is unsorted and you must answer many searches. When is sorting first worth it?
What goes wrong if you run binary search on unsorted data — does it error, or silently mislead?

technical.q: What two things must every recursive function have, and what happens in Python if the recursion goes too deep?
points: a base case that stops the recursion
each call must move toward the base case
deep recursion hits Python's recursion limit / overflows the call stack — Python does no tail-call optimisation

followups.q: What is memoisation, and which recursive function does it famously rescue?
Roughly how deep can Python recursion go by default, and what error do you get?

technical.q: BFS versus DFS on a graph: how do they differ mechanically, and when is BFS the only correct choice?
points: BFS explores level by level using a queue; DFS dives deep using a stack or recursion
BFS finds the shortest path (fewest edges) in an unweighted graph
DFS suits topological ordering, cycle detection and backtracking; memory profiles differ

followups.q: Why does DFS not guarantee the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
In an unweighted graph, why does the first time BFS reaches a node give the shortest route?

technical.q: What does it mean that Python's sort is stable, and why does that matter? Also: sorted() versus list.sort()?
points: stable = equal elements keep their original relative order
stability lets you sort by multiple keys in successive passes (least significant first)
sorted() returns a new list; list.sort() sorts in place and returns None; both are O(n log n) Timsort

followups.q: How would you sort students by grade, then by name within a grade — two ways, using stability or a key tuple?
A classic beginner bug: x = lst.sort(). What is x?

technical.q: Explain the two-pointer technique with an example, and what it improves over the brute-force approach.
points: two indices move through the data (often toward each other or as a window) instead of nested loops
classic example: pair with a target sum in a sorted array, or a sliding window over a subarray
it typically cuts O(n^2) brute force down to O(n) by never moving a pointer backwards

followups.q: In the sorted pair-sum problem, why is it safe to move the right pointer left when the sum is too big?
What property of the data makes the two-pointer trick valid for pair-sum?

technical.q: What is the difference between a primary key and a foreign key?
points: a primary key uniquely identifies a row — unique and never NULL, one per table
a foreign key stores a primary key of another table, linking rows across tables
foreign keys enforce referential integrity — no orphan references

followups.q: What should happen to orders when the customer they belong to is deleted — and which mechanisms express that?
What does referential integrity actually prevent?

technical.q: Explain INNER JOIN versus LEFT JOIN. What do you get in each result for rows with no match?
points: INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match on both sides
LEFT JOIN keeps every left row; unmatched right-side columns come back NULL
finding left rows with NO match = LEFT JOIN plus WHERE right-key IS NULL

followups.q: How would you list customers who have never placed an order, in SQL?
In a LEFT JOIN, what appears in the columns of the right table when there is no match?

technical.q: What is a database index? Why not simply index every column?
points: an index (typically a B-tree) lets the database find rows by a value without scanning the whole table
reads on indexed columns get much faster, especially joins and filters
each index costs storage and slows writes — every insert/update must maintain it

followups.q: Which columns in an orders table would you index first, and why those?
Explain the write cost: what exactly must the database update on each INSERT?

technical.q: What is normalisation trying to achieve? And when would you deliberately denormalise?
points: it removes duplicated data by splitting it into related tables
that prevents update/insert/delete anomalies — one fact, one place
denormalisation duplicates data on purpose to make hot reads faster, accepting the consistency burden

followups.q: Give me an example of an update anomaly in an un-normalised table.
In one line, what does the first normal form demand of a column's values?

technical.q: What is a transaction, and what do the four ACID properties each guarantee?
points: a transaction groups statements into one all-or-nothing unit of work
Atomicity: everything commits or everything rolls back; Consistency: the database moves between valid states
Isolation: concurrent transactions do not corrupt each other; Durability: committed data survives a crash

followups.q: Walk a bank transfer through ACID — which property saves you if the server crashes mid-transfer?
Concretely, what does rollback undo, and when does it happen automatically?

technical.q: SQL versus NoSQL: how do you decide which fits a new project?
points: relational suits structured, interrelated data and strong consistency; document/NoSQL suits flexible schemas and simple access patterns at scale
the deciding factor is the data's relationships and how it is queried, not fashion
scaling models differ: vertical + read replicas versus horizontal sharding, with consistency trade-offs

followups.q: A social feed and a payments ledger — which store for each, and what drives the difference?
What question about the data do you ask first when choosing?

technical.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
points: a process has its own private memory space; threads share the memory of their process
processes are expensive to create and isolate crashes; threads are cheap and communicate easily
threads sharing memory means race conditions — synchronisation is the programmer's problem

followups.q: If threads are cheaper and share memory, why do servers like browsers still use multiple processes?
Concretely: can two threads of one process read the same global variable? Can two processes?

technical.q: What is Python's GIL, and what does it mean for using threads on a CPU-bound task?
points: the Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time in CPython
threads still help I/O-bound work because the GIL is released while waiting
for CPU-bound parallelism in Python you use multiprocessing (separate processes, separate GILs)

followups.q: Your web scraper uses 20 threads and is fast; your image filter uses 4 threads and gains nothing. Explain both.
What does multiprocessing give up in exchange for true parallelism?

technical.q: What is a deadlock? Describe a minimal two-thread example and one way to prevent it.
points: two or more threads each hold a resource the other needs, so all wait forever (circular wait)
example: thread A locks X then wants Y; thread B locks Y then wants X
prevention: always acquire locks in the same global order (or use timeouts / one lock)

followups.q: Deadlock needs four conditions at once. Name any two and how breaking one prevents it.
Why does a fixed lock ordering actually break the circular wait?

technical.q: Explain virtual memory and paging in about a minute, as you would to a junior developer.
points: each process sees its own virtual address space, translated to physical memory in pages
pages not currently needed can live on disk; a page fault loads them on demand
if the working set exceeds RAM the system thrashes — constantly paging instead of working

followups.q: How can the sum of all processes' memory exceed the machine's RAM without everything crashing immediately?
What exactly happens, step by step, on a page fault?

technical.q: What is a context switch, why does it cost time, and who decides which process runs next?
points: a context switch saves one process/thread's CPU state and restores another's
the cost is the state save/restore plus cache/TLB disruption — the CPU does no useful work meanwhile
the OS scheduler decides, using priorities and time slices (preemptive scheduling)

followups.q: How is cooperative scheduling — like Python's asyncio — different in who decides to switch?
What state must be saved for a thread to resume exactly where it stopped?

technical.q: TCP versus UDP — what do you gain and give up with each?
points: TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered delivery with retransmission
UDP: no connection, no delivery or ordering guarantee — minimal overhead and latency
TCP for web/files/payments; UDP for live media, games and DNS where a lost packet beats a late one

followups.q: A video call uses UDP but adds its own sequencing. Why build reliability on top instead of just using TCP?
What does TCP do when a packet is lost — how does the sender find out?

technical.q: You type a URL into a browser and press Enter. Walk me through what happens, at a high level.
points: DNS resolves the hostname to an IP address (often cached)
a TCP connection opens, plus a TLS handshake for HTTPS
the browser sends an HTTP request; the server responds; the browser parses and renders, fetching sub-resources

followups.q: Where can caching happen along that path, and what does each layer save?
What exactly does DNS return, and what happens if the name does not exist?

technical.q: Which HTTP status codes should every developer know cold? Give me the meaning of 200, 201, 301, 400, 401, 403, 404 and 500.
points: 200 OK; 201 Created (usually a successful POST)
301 permanent redirect; 400 the request itself is malformed/invalid
401 unauthenticated versus 403 authenticated but not allowed; 404 resource not found; 500 the server's own error

followups.q: A user is logged in but opens an admin page. 401 or 403 — and why?
What is the practical difference between 401 and 403 for the client developer?

technical.q: What does HTTPS add over HTTP, and what does it NOT protect against?
points: TLS encrypts traffic in transit — eavesdroppers see ciphertext, not content
certificates authenticate the server's identity, so you know who you are talking to
it does not make the site itself honest or secure — a phishing site can have a valid certificate

followups.q: In the TLS handshake, how do two sides that never met end up with a shared secret over a public channel?
What is a certificate authority's role in that identity check?

technical.q: What makes an API RESTful? Describe its core ideas.
points: resources are nouns in URLs (/users/42), acted on with HTTP verbs (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE)
requests are stateless — each carries everything the server needs
responses use proper status codes and usually JSON representations

followups.q: Design the endpoints for a blog: posts and comments on posts. What do the URLs and verbs look like?
What does stateless force the client to send with every request?

technical.q: Session-based auth versus token-based (JWT) auth — how do they differ, and what are the trade-offs?
points: sessions: the server stores state and the browser holds an opaque session id in a cookie; JWT: a signed, self-contained token the server verifies without storage
sessions are easy to revoke; a JWT cannot be individually revoked before expiry without extra machinery
where the token lives matters: localStorage is readable by any script (XSS), an httpOnly cookie is not

followups.q: A user's JWT is stolen an hour before it expires. What are your options, and what does that tell you about token lifetimes?
If the server stores nothing for a JWT, how does it know the token was not forged?

technical.q: What does idempotent mean? Which HTTP methods are idempotent, and why does it matter in practice?
points: idempotent = making the same request multiple times has the same effect as making it once
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not
it makes retries safe — crucial for payments and flaky networks; POST endpoints add idempotency keys to fake it

followups.q: A payment POST times out on the client. Why is blindly retrying dangerous, and how does an idempotency key fix it?
DELETE /users/42 runs twice. What should the second call do, and is that idempotent?

technical.q: Your API endpoint gets slow as users grow toward 10,000. What are the first things you check, and in what order?
points: measure first — profile/logs to find whether the time is in the database, the app or the network
database causes first: missing indexes, N+1 queries, unbounded result sets (add pagination)
then caching for hot reads and removing repeated work — before scaling hardware

followups.q: What is an N+1 query problem, and how do you spot one in logs?
Why is an unbounded SELECT on a growing table a time bomb, and what is the standard fix?

technical.q: Why do APIs exchange JSON, and in Python what do json.loads and json.dumps each do?
points: JSON is a language-agnostic text format that maps naturally to dicts and lists
loads parses JSON text into Python objects; dumps serialises Python objects into JSON text
not everything is serialisable by default — dates, sets and custom objects need conversion

followups.q: Your API must return a datetime. What happens with plain json.dumps, and what are your options?
Mnemonic check: which of loads/dumps deals with a string, and how do you remember?

technical.q: In pandas, what is a Series versus a DataFrame, and why does the index matter?
points: a Series is one labelled 1-D column; a DataFrame is a 2-D table of Series sharing an index
operations align on the index, not on position — mismatched indexes produce NaN
vectorised operations on whole columns replace slow Python loops

followups.q: You add two Series with different indexes and get NaNs everywhere. What happened?
Why is df['x'] * 2 faster than looping over rows in pure Python?

technical.q: Explain groupby in one line, then unpack it: what are the three phases happening under the hood?
points: groupby computes a summary per group — split, apply, combine
split: rows are divided by the grouping key; apply: an aggregation runs per group
combine: the per-group results are assembled into one result indexed by the key

followups.q: groupby('city').mean() on a table with text columns — what happens to those columns, and why does it surprise people?
What is the SQL equivalent of a pandas groupby with an aggregation?

technical.q: Why do we split data into train and test sets, and what is data leakage?
points: the test set estimates performance on unseen data — tuning on the test set inflates the estimate
leakage: information from the future or from the target leaks into the features, giving impossible accuracy
defences: split before any fitting, fit preprocessing on train only, stratify for classification

followups.q: Your model scores 99% in training and 61% in production. Leakage or something else — how do you investigate?
Give me one concrete leakage example in a sales-prediction dataset.

coding.title: Second Largest (distinct)
coding.prompt: Write second_largest(nums) that returns the second-largest DISTINCT value in a list of numbers. If there is no second distinct value (empty list, one element, or all elements equal), return None.
ideaPoints: distinct values (set or track two maxima)
single pass tracking the top two, or sort the unique values
fewer than two distinct values returns None

coding.title: Two Sum
coding.prompt: Write two_sum(nums, target) that returns the indices of the two numbers that add up to target, as a list [i, j] with i < j. Exactly one solution exists, and the same element may not be used twice.
ideaPoints: hash map / dictionary of seen values
one pass
look up the complement (target - current)

coding.title: Balanced Brackets
coding.prompt: Write is_balanced(s) that returns True if every opening bracket in s — ( [ { — is closed by the matching bracket in the correct order, and False otherwise. The string contains only bracket characters.
ideaPoints: stack (LIFO)
push opening brackets, match each closing bracket against the top
stack must be empty at the end

coding.title: First Non-Repeating Character
coding.prompt: Write first_unique(s) that returns the first character of s that occurs exactly once in the string. Return an empty string if every character repeats.
ideaPoints: count occurrences with a dictionary
second pass in original order to find the first with count 1
dictionary preserves insertion order

coding.title: Reverse the Words
coding.prompt: Write reverse_words(sentence) that returns the sentence with its words in reverse order. Words are separated by single spaces, with no leading or trailing spaces.
ideaPoints: split into words
reverse the list of words (not the characters)
join with single spaces

coding.title: Group Anagrams
coding.prompt: Write group_anagrams(words) that groups the words that are anagrams of each other. Return a list of lists; the order of groups and of words inside a group does not matter.
ideaPoints: anagrams share a canonical key — their sorted letters
group with a dictionary keyed by the sorted word
character-count tuple is an alternative key

coding.title: Maximum Subarray Sum
coding.prompt: Write max_subarray(nums) that returns the largest sum of any contiguous subarray. The list has at least one number, and numbers may all be negative.
ideaPoints: Kadane's algorithm — running best-ending-here
restart the current sum when extending hurts
track the global maximum; handle all-negative by seeding with the first element

coding.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists

aptitude.q: A train travels 60 km in 45 minutes. What is its average speed?
aptitude.why: 45 minutes is 0.75 hours; 60 / 0.75 = 80 km/h.

aptitude.q: What is 15% of 240?
A shopkeeper buys an item for ₹800 and sells it for ₹920. What is the profit percentage?
aptitude.why: Profit is ₹120 on a cost of ₹800: 120/800 = 15%.

aptitude.q: What is the average of 12, 18, 20, 22 and 28?
5 workers can finish a job in 12 days. How long will 10 workers take, at the same rate?
aptitude.why: The job needs 5 × 12 = 60 worker-days; 60 / 10 = 6 days.

aptitude.q: What comes next in the series: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, …?
All cats are animals. Some animals are black. Which conclusion can be drawn for certain?
options: None of these can be concluded for certain
aptitude.why: The black animals might not include any cats — nothing about cats' colour follows for certain.

aptitude.q: Find the odd one out: 3, 5, 11, 14, 17, 21
aptitude.why: 14 is the only even number; the rest are odd.

aptitude.q: If BOOK is coded as 43 by adding the positions of its letters in the alphabet (A=1, B=2, …), what is PEN coded as?
A is B's brother. B is C's mother. How is A related to C?
aptitude.why: A is the brother of C's mother — C's maternal uncle.

aptitude.q: What comes next in the series: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …?
aptitude.why: Each term is the sum of the previous two (Fibonacci): 5 + 8 = 13.

aptitude.q: If yesterday was Friday, what day is the day after tomorrow?
aptitude.why: Yesterday Friday → today is Saturday → tomorrow Sunday → day after tomorrow is Monday.

aptitude.q: Choose the word closest in meaning to CANDID.
aptitude.why: Candid means frank — honest and direct in speech.

aptitude.q: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to SCARCE.
aptitude.why: Scarce means in short supply; abundant means plentiful.

aptitude.q: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
aptitude.why: With doesn't, the main verb stays in its base form: doesn't like.

aptitude.q: He has been working here ___ 2019.
aptitude.why: Since is used with a point in time (2019); for is used with a duration.

aptitude.q: What does the idiom 'to bite the bullet' mean?
aptitude.why: It means to endure a painful or difficult situation with courage.

aptitude.q: What is one word for 'a person who speaks many languages'?
aptitude.why: A polyglot knows or uses several languages (bilingual is exactly two).

aptitude.q: A number is increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%. What is the net change?
aptitude.why: Start with 100: +20% makes 120, then −20% of 120 is 24, leaving 96 — a 4% decrease.

aptitude.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 3 : 5 and their sum is 72. What is the larger number?
aptitude.why: 8 equal parts make 72, so one part is 9; the larger share is 5 × 9 = 45.

aptitude.q: A car covers 150 km in 2.5 hours. What is its average speed?
What is the simple interest on ₹5,000 at 8% per year for 3 years?
What is the HCF (greatest common divisor) of 24 and 36?
aptitude.why: The common divisors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12; the greatest is 12.

aptitude.q: If 3x + 7 = 25, what is x?
A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. What is the probability of drawing a red ball?
aptitude.why: 4 red out of 10 balls in total: 4/10 = 2/5.

aptitude.q: What is the perimeter of a square whose side is 9 cm?
aptitude.why: Perimeter is 4 × 9 = 36 cm (81 cm² would be the area).

aptitude.q: What is 45% of 300?
After a 10% discount, a product sells for ₹1,080. What was its original price?
The average age of 4 people is 25 years. A fifth person, aged 30, joins them. What is the new average?
aptitude.why: Total age becomes 4 × 25 + 30 = 130; 130 / 5 = 26.

aptitude.q: If a : b = 2 : 3 and b : c = 4 : 5, what is a : c?
aptitude.why: Make b equal: a : b = 8 : 12 and b : c = 12 : 15, so a : c = 8 : 15.

aptitude.q: How many minutes are there in 2.5 days?
aptitude.why: 2.5 days × 24 hours × 60 minutes = 3,600 minutes.

aptitude.q: Pipe A fills a tank in 4 hours and pipe B fills it in 6 hours. Working together, how long do they take?
aptitude.why: Together they fill 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12 of the tank per hour, so the tank takes 12/5 = 2.4 hours = 2 h 24 min.

aptitude.q: What comes next in the series: 3, 9, 27, 81, …?
aptitude.why: Each term is the previous one multiplied by 3: 81 × 3 = 243.

aptitude.q: All pens are books. All books are chairs. The conclusion 'All pens are chairs' is…
aptitude.why: Pens sit inside books and books inside chairs, so every pen is necessarily a chair — the chain is valid.

aptitude.q: Find the odd one out: 121, 144, 169, 190, 196
aptitude.why: 121, 144, 169 and 196 are perfect squares (11², 12², 13², 14²); 190 is not.

aptitude.q: If CAT is written as 3120 by joining the alphabet positions of its letters (C=3, A=1, T=20), how is DOG written?
aptitude.why: D=4, O=15, G=7, joined in order: 4157.

aptitude.q: Pointing to a photograph, Neha says: 'She is the daughter of my mother's only son.' Who is in the photograph?
aptitude.why: Neha's mother's only son is Neha's brother; his daughter is Neha's niece.

aptitude.q: What comes next in the series: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …?
aptitude.why: The terms are squares: 1², 2², 3², 4², 5², so next is 6² = 36.

aptitude.q: If 5 machines take 5 minutes to make 5 parts, how long do 100 machines take to make 100 parts?
aptitude.why: Each machine makes one part in 5 minutes; 100 machines working in parallel still take 5 minutes.

aptitude.q: A man walks 3 km north, then turns and walks 4 km east. How far is he from his starting point?
aptitude.why: The two legs form a right triangle: √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 km.

aptitude.q: Which word does not belong with the others?
aptitude.why: Apple, mango and banana are fruits; a potato is a vegetable (a tuber).

aptitude.q: If the day before yesterday was Wednesday, what day is tomorrow?
aptitude.why: Day before yesterday Wednesday → yesterday Thursday → today Friday → tomorrow is Saturday.

aptitude.q: Book is to Pages as Wall is to…
aptitude.why: A book is made up of pages; a wall is made up of bricks — part-to-whole in both pairs.

aptitude.q: In a row of 10 students, Asha is 4th from the left. What is her position from the right?
aptitude.why: Position from the right = 10 − 4 + 1 = 7th.

aptitude.q: If MANGO is coded as NZOHP by shifting each letter one step forward in the alphabet, how is APPLE coded?
aptitude.why: Shift every letter by one: A→B, P→Q, P→Q, L→M, E→F gives BQQMF.

aptitude.q: Some doctors are teachers. All teachers are singers. The conclusion 'Some doctors are singers'…
options: Follows only if all doctors are teachers
aptitude.why: The doctors who are teachers are singers, because every teacher is a singer — so some doctors are certainly singers.

aptitude.q: Choose the word closest in meaning to RAPID.
aptitude.why: Rapid means very fast — swift.

aptitude.q: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to ANCIENT.
aptitude.why: Ancient means very old; its opposite here is modern.

aptitude.q: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Neither of the answers are correct.
Neither of the answers is correct.
Neither of the answers be correct.
Neither of the answers were correct.
aptitude.why: 'Neither' is singular, so it takes the singular verb 'is'.

aptitude.q: She is very good ___ mathematics.
aptitude.why: The fixed phrase is 'good at' a subject or skill.

aptitude.q: What does the idiom 'a blessing in disguise' mean?
aptitude.why: It is something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good — a hidden benefit.

aptitude.q: What is one word for 'a place where birds are kept'?
aptitude.why: An aviary houses birds; an apiary keeps bees and an aquarium keeps fish.

aptitude.q: Choose the word closest in meaning to BRIEF.
aptitude.why: Brief means short in duration or length.

aptitude.q: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to EXPAND.
aptitude.why: Expand means to become larger; contract means to become smaller.

aptitude.q: Which word is spelt correctly?
aptitude.why: Occurred doubles both the c and the r: o-c-c-u-r-r-e-d.

aptitude.q: By the time we reached the station, the train ___ already left.
aptitude.why: The leaving happened before another past event, so the past perfect 'had left' is used.

aptitude.q: What does the idiom 'to hit the books' mean?
aptitude.why: To hit the books means to begin studying seriously.

aptitude.q: What is one word for 'that which cannot be heard'?
aptitude.why: Inaudible means impossible to hear; illegible means impossible to read.

aptitude.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
aptitude.why: 'It's' with an apostrophe is the contraction of 'it is'; 'its' without one shows possession.

aptitude.q: He apologised ___ his mistake.
aptitude.why: The fixed phrase is 'apologise for' something you did wrong.

gdTopics.title: Artificial intelligence in classrooms — a tool or a threat?
gdTopics.brief: Schools and colleges are split on whether AI tools help students learn or simply do the learning for them.

voices.name: Aarav
voices.open: I think AI in classrooms is clearly a tool. A student stuck at midnight gets an explanation instantly instead of waiting two days for a doubt session. Used well, it personalises learning the way no single teacher with sixty students can.
voices.follow: I'd add that the threat framing assumes students only copy. The same was said about calculators — the answer was to change what we test, not ban the tool.

voices.name: Meera
voices.open: I'm cautious. If the AI writes the essay and solves the problem set, the student practises nothing. Learning is the struggle itself — remove it and you get graduates who can prompt but cannot think.
voices.follow: And there's an honesty problem too. Teachers can't tell genuine work from generated work anymore, so assessment itself is breaking down.

voices.name: Kabir
voices.open: I sit in the middle: it depends entirely on how it's deployed. AI as a tutor that asks questions is very different from AI as an answer machine. The institution's rules decide which one shows up.
voices.follow: Exactly — policy is the real topic here. Allow it for drafting and doubts, ban it in exams, and teach students to verify what it says.

gdTopics.close: We've heard the main positions — tool, threat, and 'it depends on the rules'. Final thoughts are welcome before we wrap up.

gdTopics.title: Should freshers prefer startups or large companies?
gdTopics.brief: A classic fresher dilemma: the learning speed and ownership of a startup versus the structure and brand of a large company.

voices.name: Meera
voices.open: For a fresher, a startup is a fast-forward button. You ship real code in week one, sit with founders, and learn in one year what takes three in a large company. Early career is for learning speed, not comfort.
voices.follow: Brand names matter less than people think — recruiters ask what you built, and at a startup you actually built things.

voices.name: Kabir
voices.open: I'd argue the opposite. A fresher doesn't know what good engineering looks like yet. Large companies teach process, code review, scale — the discipline that makes the startup chaos survivable later.
voices.follow: And let's be honest about risk: most startups fail or pay late. A first job also has to pay the rent reliably.

voices.name: Aarav
voices.open: Both of you assume the company type decides everything. The team and the manager matter more. A great mentor at a boring company beats a chaotic startup with no guidance, every time.
voices.follow: I'd judge the offer by one question: who will review my work and teach me in the first six months? Everything else is secondary.

gdTopics.close: Startups for speed, large companies for structure, and the mentor question cutting across both — a good place to land your final view.

gdTopics.title: Remote work or office work for early-career engineers?
gdTopics.brief: Many companies now hire freshers into hybrid or fully remote roles. Is that a gift or a handicap at the start of a career?

voices.name: Kabir
voices.open: Remote is a gift. A fresher from a small town gets a metro salary without metro rent, and deep-work hours at home beat an open-plan office for actual coding. The savings in year one are life-changing.
voices.follow: The mentorship argument is real but solvable — pair programming over a call and good written culture teach plenty, if the team bothers.

voices.name: Aarav
voices.open: For the first two years, office wins and it's not close. You learn by overhearing seniors debug, by the corridor question that saves you a day. Remote freshers often stay invisible and plateau quietly.
voices.follow: Visibility matters for growth too — promotions go to people the leads actually know and trust.

voices.name: Meera
voices.open: This is why hybrid exists. Two or three office days for mentorship and bonding, remote days for focus and savings. The mistake is treating it as all-or-nothing.
voices.follow: Though I'd say the fresher shouldn't choose by policy alone — a fully remote team with strong rituals can out-teach a lazy office.

gdTopics.close: Savings and focus on one side, mentorship and visibility on the other, hybrid in between — final positions, please.

gdTopics.title: Social media does more harm than good for students.
gdTopics.brief: Attention, comparison, misinformation on one side; community, learning and opportunity on the other.

voices.name: Aarav
voices.open: I agree with the statement. The platforms are engineered to steal attention — the average student loses hours daily to feeds designed against their interests. Add comparison anxiety and misinformation, and the harm ledger is longer.
voices.follow: The learning argument is weak too — for every good tutorial there are fifty distractions one swipe away, and the algorithm promotes the distractions.

voices.name: Kabir
voices.open: I disagree. The same platforms run the study communities, internship alerts and open-source showcases that got half my class placed. The tool isn't the harm — unregulated use is, and that's teachable.
voices.follow: Also, for students outside big cities, social media IS the network. It levels access to mentors and opportunities that used to need connections.

voices.name: Meera
voices.open: The statement is too sweeping. Harm and good run on the same rails; what differs is the student's intent — consumption versus creation. A student posting projects gains; a student only scrolling pays.
voices.follow: I'd put responsibility on design too — if a platform profits from addiction, self-control alone is an unfair ask of a sixteen-year-old.

gdTopics.close: Harm, good, and the intent question — we've circled the statement well. Your closing take?

gdTopics.title: Degrees vs skills — what should hiring value more?
gdTopics.brief: Employers increasingly list 'skills-based hiring' while still filtering by degree. Which signal deserves more weight?

voices.name: Meera
voices.open: Skills, plainly. A degree certifies attendance across four years; a portfolio demonstrates the actual job. When a candidate shows real projects and passes a work-sample test, the degree adds almost no information.
voices.follow: Degrees also filter out late bloomers and self-taught talent — exactly the hungry candidates companies claim to want.

voices.name: Aarav
voices.open: I'll defend the degree a little. It signals sustained effort, foundational theory, and the ability to finish something hard over years. Skills tests can be gamed in a weekend; four years of coursework is harder to fake.
voices.follow: And in fields like core engineering or research, the theory IS the skill — you can't portfolio your way past thermodynamics.

voices.name: Kabir
voices.open: I think the honest answer is: degree as a floor for some roles, skills as the decider for all. Use the degree to check foundations if you must, but let the work sample make the final call.
voices.follow: Companies say skills-first but filter degree-first because it's cheap. The ones who actually test skills get the better hires — the data from their own funnels shows it.

gdTopics.close: Skills as proof, degrees as signal, and the funnel argument on the table — last word to you.

gdTopics.title: Electric vehicles are the future of Indian roads.
gdTopics.brief: EV sales are rising, charging infrastructure is thin, and petrol is familiar. Is the transition inevitable?

voices.name: Kabir
voices.open: The transition is inevitable. Running costs are a fifth of petrol, city pollution is a public-health emergency, and every major manufacturer has committed. Two-wheelers alone — most of India's vehicles — are already flipping fast.
voices.follow: Charging anxiety shrinks every year; battery swapping for two-wheelers is already working in several cities.

voices.name: Meera
voices.open: I'd slow down. Our electricity is still largely coal-generated, batteries are imported, and a family in a small town can't charge on a highway trip today. 'Future' yes — but the timeline being sold is fantasy.
voices.follow: There's also the disposal question nobody answers: millions of dead batteries need a recycling system that doesn't exist yet at scale.

voices.name: Aarav
voices.open: Both are right by segment. City two-wheelers and fleet cars: electric wins today. Long-haul trucks and rural use: not yet. India's EV story will be won segment by segment, not in one wave.
voices.follow: Policy should match that — subsidise where the economics already work instead of spreading thin everywhere.

gdTopics.close: Inevitable, premature, or segment-by-segment — bring us home with your final position.
